title: The loop lands each ticket as it finishes

statements.says: Each ticket is built in a throwaway worktree of its own, branched from the newest origin/main.
Each ticket lands on main the moment it passes.
The worktree is removed when the ticket passes and stays when it fails, so a broken state can be read.
The main checkout stays clean for the whole run, and two loops on two specs can work at once.
The thing that must be whole is the ticket, and the checks that say so run before its push.
The rebase is verified by command rather than by asking the agent how it went.
The full suite is re-run whenever the base moved.
A push that lost a race is retried a bounded number of times.
The session that wrote the ticket resolves a rebase conflict, and the driver hands it the commits that landed, the ticket behind each one, and each of those tickets' Closing notes.
The resolving session refuses when the answer is in neither side and in neither ticket.
The resolving session refuses when the project's checks are still failing after one attempt to fix them.
A refusal leaves the conflict alone, says which side wanted what, and stops; it never means resolve badly.
A refusal stops the whole loop.
Each conflict's size and outcome is logged.
A loop commit names its ticket, in a trailer that does not close the issue.
A ticket is closed with a comment naming the commit.
The issue tracker doc states both conventions.
A loop commit stops naming its ticket with GitHub's closing words, such as Closes #n.
Older commits stay untraceable; the convention covers future loop commits only.
git reset --hard no longer undoes a run; undoing a landed ticket is a revert like any other change.
The spec's drift check and the close offer are unchanged.
A ticket the drift check later questions is already pushed, so answering it is a new commit rather than an edit to work still sitting at home.
Working in the one checkout left it dirty for the whole run, so the developer could not read a file without seeing edits, try anything, or start a second loop.
Pushing once at the end meant a spec that stopped on its eighth ticket left seven finished tickets on one machine.
The spec does not have to be whole, a ticket does, and finished work sitting on one machine is at the mercy of that machine.
The old rule made undoing a run a single git reset --hard, a convenience for the rare abandoned run paid for on every run that succeeds.
The worktree makes the per-ticket push cheap, because the rebase it needs is already happening.
The session that wrote the ticket resolves the conflict because half of it is already in its head.
Gathering the commits and tickets first makes a refusal honest, since an agent can only say the answer is in neither ticket once the tickets were in front of it.
A refusal stops the loop because every stop says something about how to improve the loop, and a parked ticket is a stop nobody sees.
The resolution reads a commit message to find its ticket and that ticket's Closing note to find the intention, so neither convention may lapse.
GitHub's closing words close an issue with no comment.
The Closing note is the richest source of intention in the repository.
Each conflict's size and outcome is logged so a threshold can later be set from this repository's own numbers.
Counted across the history, only about two commits in five could be traced from the message, and the habit had been lapsing.
Taking the worktree and keeping the one push was rejected, because finished work would then sit on a branch nobody is looking at as well as on one machine.
Parking a failed ticket and carrying on was rejected, because it trades a stop the developer sees for one they do not.

Limiting the size of a conflict an agent may attempt was rejected, because the published threshold comes from a narrow 2020 model and refusing early saves nothing when a refusal stops the loop anyway.
Holding a lock across landing was rejected, because it would block the other loop for minutes across a full test run to prevent a collision lasting seconds.
Closing the ticket from the commit message was rejected, because it closes the issue with no comment, and the Closing note is what a resolving agent reads.
It replaces the driver's earlier rule that the loop commits per ticket and pushes once at the end.
The record landed before the code that leans on it, and that code has since arrived: the loop script, the implement skill and the README now say what the record says.
Its rejection of a lock across landing has since been replaced by a later record, because the logs proved the bounded retry did not answer the push race.
